approaches.name: Copy the values, write them back reversed
approaches.idea: Read the values into an array, then walk the list again writing the values from the back of the array.
steps: Walk the list and append each value to an array.
Walk the list again; write `values[n − 1]`, `values[n − 2]`, … into the nodes.
Return `head` (the same first node, now holding the last value).
approaches.why: Two passes; the array holds n values. It changes values rather than links, which interviewers usually do not accept.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Reverse the rest of the list first; then the node after `head` is the tail of that reversed part, so hang `head` after it.
steps: If `head` is null or has no next node, return `head`.
Reverse the rest: `newHead = reverseList(head.next)`.
Set `head.next.next = head` and `head.next = null`.
Return `newHead`.
approaches.why: One call per node; the call stack is n frames deep, which can overflow on very long lists.

approaches.name: Iterative reversal with three pointers
approaches.idea: Walk the list once, turning each node's `next` pointer back towards the previous node. Save the following node first so it is not lost.
steps: Set `prev = null`, `cur = head`.
While `cur` is not null: save `next = cur.next`, set `cur.next = prev`, then `prev = cur`, `cur = next`.
Return `prev`, the old tail and new head.
approaches.why: One pass with three pointers; no recursion stack.

merge-two-sorted-lists.pattern: Two-pointer merge with a dummy head

approaches.name: Collect all values, sort, build a new list
approaches.idea: Ignore that the lists are already sorted: gather every value, sort, and create fresh nodes.
steps: Append all values of both lists to an array.
Sort the array.
Build a new list from the sorted values and return its head.
approaches.why: The sort dominates; the array and the new nodes take O(n + m). It also breaks the rule of reusing the existing nodes.

approaches.name: Recursive merge
approaches.idea: The smaller of the two front nodes comes first; its `next` is the merge of everything that remains.
steps: If either list is empty, return the other.
If `list1.val <= list2.val`, set `list1.next = merge(list1.next, list2)` and return `list1`.
Otherwise set `list2.next = merge(list1, list2.next)` and return `list2`.
approaches.why: One call per node placed; the recursion goes n + m frames deep.

approaches.name: Iterative merge with a dummy node
approaches.idea: Build the result behind a dummy node: repeatedly attach the smaller front node, and attach whatever remains when one list runs out.
steps: Create `dummy` and set `tail = dummy`.
While both lists are non-empty, attach the smaller front node to `tail`, advance that list, and advance `tail`.
Attach the non-empty remainder (if any) in one step: `tail.next = list1 or list2`.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: Each node is attached once; only the dummy and a tail pointer are extra.

approaches.name: Build a new list of the values to keep
approaches.idea: Walk the list and copy every value that is not `val` into a brand-new list.
steps: Create a dummy node and a `tail` pointer.
For each node whose value is not `val`, append a new node with that value.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: One pass, but it allocates up to n new nodes instead of reusing the existing ones.

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Clean the rest of the list first, then decide whether the current node stays.
steps: If `head` is null, return null.
Set `head.next = removeElements(head.next, val)`.
Return `head.next` if `head.val == val`, otherwise `head`.
approaches.why: One call per node; the call stack is n deep.

approaches.name: Dummy node and in-place unlinking
approaches.idea: Put a dummy node before the head so every node, including the head, has a predecessor. Then skip over matching nodes by relinking.
steps: Create `dummy` with `dummy.next = head`; set `prev = dummy`.
While `prev.next` is not null: if `prev.next.val == val`, set `prev.next = prev.next.next` (do not move `prev`, the new next may match too); otherwise move `prev` forward.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: Each node is looked at once; only the dummy and one pointer are extra.

add-two-numbers.pattern: Digit-by-digit addition with a carry, building the result behind a dummy node

approaches.name: Copy the digits into arrays, add, then build the list
approaches.idea: Converting to a built-in integer fails (numbers have up to 100 digits), so copy the digits into arrays and do schoolbook addition there, then turn the result into a list.
steps: Copy the digits of `l1` and `l2` into arrays `a` and `b` (ones digit first).
For `i` from 0 to `max(len) − 1`, add `a[i] + b[i] + carry` (missing digits count as 0); store the last digit and keep the carry.
If a carry remains, add it as a final digit.
Build a list from the result digits and return it.
approaches.why: A few linear passes; the two digit arrays are extra O(n + m) memory that the direct approach avoids.

approaches.name: Walk both lists adding with a carry
approaches.idea: The lists already hold the ones digit first, which is the order schoolbook addition works in. Walk both together, add digit + digit + carry, and append the last digit of that sum.
steps: Create `dummy`, `tail = dummy`, `carry = 0`.
While `l1`, `l2` or `carry` is non-zero: `s = carry + (l1 ? l1.val : 0) + (l2 ? l2.val : 0)`.
Append a node with `s % 10`, set `carry = s / 10`, and advance whichever lists are not finished.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: One step per digit of the longer number (plus one for a final carry). Apart from the output list, only the carry and a few pointers are used.

reverse-linked-list-ii.pattern: Sublist reversal in one pass (head insertion behind a fixed predecessor)

approaches.name: Copy values, reverse the slice, write back
approaches.idea: Read all values into an array, reverse positions `left..right` there, and write the values back into the nodes.
steps: Copy the values into an array.
Reverse the array between indices `left − 1` and `right − 1`.
Walk the list again and write the array values back in order; return `head`.
approaches.why: A few linear passes and an array of n values. It swaps values rather than links.

approaches.name: One pass: move each node to the front of the sublist
approaches.idea: Stop at the node before position `left` (`prev`). The node at `left` (`cur`) will end up last in the reversed part; repeatedly take the node right after `cur` and insert it directly after `prev`.
steps: Create `dummy` before `head`; walk `prev` forward `left − 1` steps from `dummy`.
Set `cur = prev.next`.
Repeat `right − left` times: `move = cur.next`; `cur.next = move.next`; `move.next = prev.next`; `prev.next = move`.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: At most `right` steps in a single pass, each with O(1) relinking. The dummy covers `left = 1`, where the head changes.

swap-nodes-in-pairs.pattern: Pointer rewiring in fixed-size groups (dummy head)

approaches.name: Recursion
approaches.idea: Swap the first two nodes, and let the recursive call handle the rest of the list.
steps: If fewer than two nodes remain, return `head`.
Let `second = head.next`; set `head.next = swapPairs(second.next)`.
Set `second.next = head` and return `second`.
approaches.why: One call per pair: n/2 calls, so the stack is O(n) deep.

approaches.name: Iterative with a dummy node
approaches.idea: Keep `prev` just before the next pair. Rewire three links to put the pair's second node first, then move `prev` to the pair's new second node.
steps: Create `dummy` before `head`; set `prev = dummy`.
While `prev.next` and `prev.next.next` exist: `a = prev.next`, `b = a.next`.
Rewire: `a.next = b.next`, `b.next = a`, `prev.next = b`; then `prev = a`.
Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: Each pair is rewired once with three pointer changes; no recursion.

partition-list.pattern: Split into two lists behind two dummy heads, then join them

approaches.name: Collect the nodes into two arrays
approaches.idea: Put nodes with values below `x` in one array and the rest in another, each in original order, then relink them in that order.
steps: Walk the list, appending each node to `small` or `large`.
Concatenate `small` and `large` and link each node to the next one; the last node points to null.
Return the first node (or null for an empty list).
approaches.why: Two linear passes; the arrays hold n node references.

approaches.name: Two dummy-headed lists
approaches.idea: Grow two lists as you walk: one for values below `x`, one for the rest. Appending at the tail keeps each group's order. Finally link the end of the first to the start of the second.
steps: Create dummies `lessHead` and `moreHead` with tails `less` and `more`.
For each node, append it to `less` if its value is below `x`, else to `more`.
Set `more.next = null` (the last node may still point into the old list) and `less.next = moreHead.next`.
Return `lessHead.next`.
approaches.why: One pass; only two dummies and two tails are extra. Forgetting to end the second list creates a cycle.

rotate-list.pattern: Close the list into a ring, then cut it at the new tail (k mod length)

approaches.name: Move the last node to the front, k mod n times
approaches.idea: One rotation step moves the tail to the front. Rotating n times returns the original list, so only `k mod n` steps are needed; do them one by one.
steps: If the list is empty, return it. Count its length `n` and set `k = k mod n`.
Repeat `k` times: walk to the second-to-last node, detach the last node, and put it in front of `head`.
Return `head`.
approaches.why: Up to n − 1 rotation steps, each walking the list. Without the `mod n` it would be O(k·n) with k up to 2 × 10⁹.

approaches.name: Make a ring, then cut it
approaches.idea: Rotating right by `k` makes node `n − k` (counting from 0) the new head. Join the tail to the head to form a ring, walk to the new tail, and break the ring there.
steps: If the list is empty or has one node, return it. Find the tail and the length `n` in one pass.
Set `k = k mod n`; if it is 0, return `head`.
Link `tail.next = head` to make a ring.
Walk `n − k − 1` steps from `head` to reach the new tail; the new head is the node after it. Cut: `newTail.next = null`; return the new head.
approaches.why: One pass to measure and at most one more partial pass to find the cut; a few pointers of state.

reverse-nodes-in-k-group.pattern: Reverse fixed-size groups in place, reconnecting each group to the previous one

approaches.name: Recursion, one group per call
approaches.idea: Check that k nodes are available; if so, reverse those k nodes, and attach the result of recursively processing the rest of the list to the end of the reversed group.
steps: Walk k nodes from `head`; if the list ends first, return `head` unchanged.
Reverse the first k nodes with the usual prev/cur loop; `head` becomes the group's last node.
Set `head.next = reverseKGroup(nextGroupStart, k)`.
Return the group's new first node (`prev`).
approaches.why: Each node is visited twice (counting and reversing). One call per group means n/k stack frames, which breaks the O(1) memory rule.

approaches.name: Iterative, group by group behind a dummy node
approaches.idea: Keep `groupPrev`, the node just before the next group. If k nodes follow it, reverse them in place, hook the reversed group between `groupPrev` and the rest, and move `groupPrev` to the group's new last node.
steps: Create `dummy` before `head`; set `groupPrev = dummy`.
Find `kth`, the k-th node after `groupPrev`; if it does not exist, stop.
Reverse the nodes from `groupPrev.next` to `kth`, starting `prev` at `kth.next` so the group's old first node ends up pointing to the rest of the list.
Set `first = groupPrev.next` (old first, now last), `groupPrev.next = kth`, then `groupPrev = first`, and repeat. Return `dummy.next`.
approaches.why: Each node is visited a constant number of times (finding `kth` and reversing); only a handful of pointers are used.

insert-greatest-common-divisors-in-linke.pattern: Insert after the current node, then skip the new one

approaches.name: GCD by trying divisors
approaches.idea: Walk the list and insert a node between each pair, finding the GCD by testing candidates from the smaller value downwards.
steps: For each node `a` with a next node `b`: let `g` start at `min(a.val, b.val)` and decrease it until it divides both.
Insert a node with value `g` between `a` and `b`, then move `a` to `b`.
approaches.why: V is the largest value (1000). The trial-division GCD costs up to V steps per pair, so this is fine here but grows with the values. Output nodes are not counted as extra space.

approaches.name: Euclid's GCD
approaches.idea: Same walk, but compute each GCD with Euclid's algorithm: `gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a mod b)`.
steps: For each node `a` with a next node `b`, compute `g = gcd(a.val, b.val)` with Euclid.
Set `a.next = new node(g, b)` and continue from `b`, skipping the inserted node.
approaches.why: Euclid's algorithm takes O(log V) steps because the remainder at least halves every two steps. Jumping straight to `b` matters: advancing one node at a time would land on the new node and insert endlessly.

copy-list-with-random-pointer.pattern: Old-to-new node map (or interleave copies in place)

approaches.name: Copy by position
approaches.idea: Copy the values and `next` links into an array of new nodes, then, for each original random pointer, find its position by walking the original list from the head.
steps: Put the original nodes in a list `orig` and create `copy[i]` for each, linking `copy[i].next = copy[i + 1]`.
For each `i` with `orig[i].random != null`, scan `orig` to find the index `j` of that node.
Set `copy[i].random = copy[j]` and return `copy[0]`.
approaches.why: Finding each random target by scanning costs O(n), so the whole copy is quadratic. It works because node identity (not value) is compared, which matters when values repeat.

approaches.name: Hash map from old node to new node
approaches.idea: First pass: create a copy of every node and store `old → new`. Second pass: wire each copy's `next` and `random` through the map.
steps: For each original node `t`, put `map[t] = new Node(t.val)`.
For each `t`, set `map[t].next = map[t.next]` and `map[t].random = map[t.random]` (with `map[null] = null`).
Return `map[head]`.
approaches.why: Two linear passes with O(1) map lookups. The map is the clean, interview-friendly answer and also works for general graphs (Clone Graph is the same idea).

approaches.name: Interleave copies, then split
approaches.idea: Put each copy directly after its original: `A → A' → B → B' …`. Then the copy of `X.random` is simply `X.random.next`, so no map is needed. Finally pull the two lists apart.
steps: Weave: for each original `t`, insert `new Node(t.val)` between `t` and `t.next`.
Randoms: for each original `t`, set `t.next.random = t.random == null ? null : t.random.next`.
Split: restore `t.next = t.next.next` for each original and link each copy to the next copy. Return the first copy.
approaches.why: Three linear passes and no extra structure besides the output. The original list must be fully restored at the end; the judge checks that the copy shares no node with it.
